answer.rationale: Rollback (memory_b1) is off the table: compliance has ruled the security patch cannot be reverted, so the strongest historical precedent is unavailable regardless of how well it worked on day 18. Regional failover (memory_b2) recovered latency fast in March, but that was a regional degradation with shiftable traffic; here we are at settlement peak with heavy in-flight writes, and a failover under write pressure is the single most likely way to actually lose customer writes — which the primary objective forbids. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) worked when the failure was an external partner dependency and failing fast preserved the rest of the path; here the write path itself is the degraded component, so tripping the breaker sheds exactly the writes we are trying to protect. Added capacity (memory_b3) was provisioned ahead of a known peak; provisioning now, 90 minutes into a live climb, likely lands after the peak has passed. That leaves read-replica routing (memory_b5), which is the only candidate that reduces load on the primary without discarding or interrupting writes, and it is reversible. I want to verify memory_b5 because the summary is thin on the causal mechanism: it says report queries were moved and write latency recovered, but not whether the primary was actually read-saturated in that incident, nor how much of the 5x we should expect it to absorb. If the day-55 record shows the win came from a specific heavy dashboard workload we do not currently have, the expected benefit here collapses and I would rather know that before committing my one intervention. I am holding real uncertainty about causation: the climb began roughly when the release shipped two hours ago, and read offload does nothing about a regression in the new build — it buys headroom, not a diagnosis. So I am running this as a small guarded test on a bounded slice of report/read traffic with the primary's write p99 as the readout, not a broad cutover, so that a null result still leaves the next window open. Downstream value risk: shifting reads to replicas introduces replica lag into anything that reads-then-writes, and in a payments and settlement path stale reads can produce duplicate or incorrect ledger entries — a correctness failure that is worse than the latency it fixes. Any routing must exclude read-for-write and settlement-critical queries and stay on the primary for those.
